system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with HCV-related cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and a history of TIPS placement, was admitted for coffee ground emesis and melena, concerning for upper GI bleeding. His symptoms resolved, and recent endoscopic findings suggested portal hypertensive gastropathy and esophagitis as likely sources. He underwent a TIPS revision with balloon dilation, reducing the portosystemic gradient from 20 to 13 mmHg, and sclerotherapy of gastric varices. Two therapeutic paracenteses removed 7L and 4L of fluid, with no evidence of infection. He was managed with octreotide, pantoprazole, and ciprofloxacin prophylaxis. Hyponatremia was monitored and remained stable. His insulin was adjusted, and glipizide was held. Palliative care was consulted per patient request. He improved clinically, with stable vital signs and labs, and was discharged home with follow-up plans, medication adjustments, and recommendations to restart aspirin when bleeding risk decreases.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with recent TIPS and recurrent bleeding.  //
Please perform TIPS revision with embolization of residual varices.

COMPARISON:  Portal venogram ___, TIPS ultrasound ___, TIPS
placement ___.

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___ resident, Dr. ___
radiologist, and Dr. ___ radiologist performed the procedure.
Dr. ___ supervised the trainee during the key components of
the procedure and has reviewed and agrees with the trainee's findings.
ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
100mcg of fentanyl and 2 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 130 minutes during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine
was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS:  None.
CONTRAST: 125 ml of Optiray contrast.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  38.1 min, 631 mGy

PROCEDURE:  1. Paracentesis
2. Right internal jugular venous access using ultrasound.
3. Pre-procedure right atrial and main portal vein pressure measurements.
4. Contrast enhanced portal venogram.
5.  Occlusion of a gastric varix with alcohol sclerosis and Amplatzer plug
placement.
6.  Balloon angioplasty of the TIPS shunt with an 8 mm balloon.
8.  Post-angioplasty portal venogram.
9.  Post-angioplasty right atrial and main portal vein pressure measurements.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed
supine on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___
protocol. The right neck and right abdomen was prepped and draped in the usual
sterile fashion.
Under ultrasound guidance and after the instillation of 1% lidocaine into the
superficial soft tissues, a 5 ___ ___ needle was advanced into a large
pocket of ascites in the right lower quadrant.  5L of slightly cloudy yellow
fluid was removed.
Under continuous ultrasound guidance, the patent right internal jugular vein
was compressible and accessed using a micropuncture needle.  Images of
ultrasound access were stored on PACS. Subsequently a Nitinol wire was passed
into the right atrium using fluoroscopic guidance. A small incision was made
at the needle entry site. The needle was exchanged for a micropuncture sheath.
The Nitinol wire was removed and a ___ wire was advanced distally into
the IVC.
The micropuncture sheath was then removed and a 6 ___ x 25 cm sheath was
advanced over the wire into the inferior vena cava. ___ wire and a
Kumpe catheter, access was obtained through the TIPS shunt into the main
portal vein.  The ___ wire was exchanged for a Glidewire, and with the help
of the Kumpe catheter, was advanced into the splenic vein.  The Kumpe catheter
was exchanged for straight flush catheter, and a portal venogram was
performed, with findings discussed below.  Subsequently, the straight flush
catheter was exchanged for a C2 catheter, which was used with the Glidewire to
select a large gastric varix.  A venogram was performed from this location,
with findings discussed below.  Then, the varix was sclerosed using 5 cc of
absolute ethanol.  Subsequently, there was some flow still remaining in the
varix, and an 8 mm Amplatzer plug was placed.  Afterwards, there was no
subsequent flow through the varix.  The catheter was withdrawn into the
splenic vein and exchanged for a straight flush catheter, and a repeat portal
venogram was obtained, with findings discussed below.  Then, attention was
turned to a varix which appeared to arise from the region of the TIPS and
course caudally.  Multiple attempts was made to gain access into this varix
using a SOS catheter and a Glidewire, which were unsuccessful.  Then,
correlation with MRI imaging revealed that this varix was coursing to the
anterior abdominal wall and not to bowel, therefore not responsible for GI
bleeding.

Then, attention was turned to the TIPS shunt.  Given the history of hepatic
encephalopathy, the TIPS shunt was dilated using an 8 mm balloon.  Post
angioplasty venogram was performed, with findings discussed below.  Post
intervention right atrial and main portal vein pressure measurements were
obtained, with findings discussed below.

The sheath was then removed from the right internal jugular vein site and
pressure held for 10 minutes to achieve hemostasis. Steri-strips and sterile
dressings were applied.
The patient tolerated the procedure well.  There were no immediate
post-procedure complications. The patient was transferred to the PACU in
stable condition.

FINDINGS: 

1. Pre-TIPS right atrial pressure of 8 mm Hg and main portal vein pressure
measurement of 23 mm Hg resulting in portosystemic gradient of 15 mmHg.
2. Contrast enhanced portal venogram showing a large gastric varix shunting
into the IVC.
4.  Post sclerosis and plug embolization of the gastric varix shows no more
filling of this varix.  A large varix arising near the TIPS was noted,
coursing caudally.  Correlation with MRI imaging demonstrates that this varix
courses to the anterior abdominal wall and not to bowel.
5.  Post balloon-angioplasty venogram of the TIPS shows reduced filling of the
large anterior abdominal wall varix.
5. Post-TIPS right atrial pressure of 13 mm Hg and portal pressure of 23 mm Hg
resulting in portosystemic gradient of 10 mmHg.
6.  5 liters of cloudy yellow fluid removed through right paracentesis drain.

IMPRESSION: 

1. Successful right internal jugular access with gastric varix sclerosis with
alcohol and embolization with Amplatzer plug.
2. Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt balloon-angioplasty with
subsequent decrease in porto-systemic pressure gradient to 10 mm Hg, compared
to 15 mm Hg pre intervention.
3. 5 liters of ascites was drained.

RECOMMENDATION(S):  The TIPS shunt may be dilated further to 9 or 10mm if
necessary to control bleeding or ascites.  The reason for the slow incremental
dilation of the shunt is the concern for development of recurrent
encephalopathy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You came in with chest pain and vomiting blood. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve had this burning feeling in my chest, especially when I lie down. It started yesterday. Then today, I threw up dark red blood—maybe half a cup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned it feels like heartburn. Did antacids help at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little, but not much. I think I ran out of my Protonix about 10 days ago. I meant to refill it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Being off your acid-reducing medication may have contributed. We’ve started you on an IV version to help protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is that why I bled?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. With your history of cirrhosis and portal hypertension, you’re at risk for bleeding from varices or from a condition called portal hypertensive gastropathy. We’ll do an endoscopy to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. They found bleeding in my stomach last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and you’ve had a TIPS procedure in the past. We’re concerned it might not be working as well, which could increase pressure and lead to bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So they might need to fix it again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely. We’ll do an EGD first to see where the bleeding is, then possibly a TIPS revision if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, we did the endoscopy. Good news—no active bleeding. We saw esophagitis and signs of portal hypertensive gastropathy, but no varices in the esophagus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not from the big veins?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not this time. The stomach lining is inflamed due to high pressure from your liver disease. But we also found a hiatal hernia, which could explain the chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the chest pain and bleeding are related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The same high pressure affects both. We’re keeping you on IV pantoprazole and octreotide to reduce that pressure and protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the TIPS?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked with an ultrasound. The TIPS is open, but flow is turbulent. We’re planning a revision tomorrow to improve it and reduce the risk of future bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they do something about the fluid in my belly too? I feel so bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. During the TIPS procedure, they’ll also drain some fluid—called a paracentesis—to make you more comfortable and check for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your sodium is low at 127, but stable. We’re keeping you on a 1.5-liter fluid restriction to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if it drops further, but we’re monitoring it closely. It’s common with advanced liver disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my breathing? I feel a little tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows small fluid collections—likely from your liver disease, called hepatic hydrothorax. They’ve improved since yesterday, so we’ll keep watching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, you had the TIPS revision yesterday. It went well. They used a balloon to widen the shunt and placed a plug in a bleeding gastric varix.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did it help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The pressure in your liver veins dropped from 15 to 10 mmHg, which is good. They also drained 5 liters of fluid from your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Five liters? That’s a lot!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is. But the fluid showed no signs of infection, which is excellent. You should feel less bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do, actually. What about my heart? I was worried about the chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your heart enzymes twice—both were normal. No sign of a heart attack. The pain is likely from the esophagitis and hiatal hernia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. What about my diabetes? I didn’t get my glyburide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held glyburide because it can cause low blood sugar, especially with poor intake. We’re using insulin instead to keep your sugars stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And my liver cancer? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your last imaging showed stable lesions. We recommend follow-up liver imaging next month to monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got the CT scan results. No pneumothorax. The odd spot on your X-ray was just an artifact. Your lungs show some atelectasis, but no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about a collapsed lung.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understandable, but the CT ruled it out. You’re safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show your hemoglobin is stable at 8.7. You got a unit of blood earlier, and it helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If all goes well, tomorrow. We’ll make sure you’re eating, your vitals are stable, and your labs don’t drop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds will I go home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pantoprazole twice a day, sucralfate for two weeks, and your usual lactulose, rifaximin, and insulin. We’ll restart glyburide when you're eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Protonix? I won’t forget it again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Staying on it is key to preventing another bleed. We’re giving you a 60-day supply.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll set a reminder. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your hepatologist in two weeks. Also, palliative care as an outpatient—they can help with symptom management and planning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your labs are stable, you’re eating well, and your breathing is better. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take your meds, limit fluids, and call if you have fever, confusion, or any bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll make those follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, Mr. ___.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with HCV-related cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and a history of TIPS and recurrent liver cancer, was admitted for hematemesis and chest pain. He had been off his pantoprazole for 10 days, which likely contributed to upper GI bleeding from portal hypertensive gastropathy and esophagitis. He underwent a TIPS revision with balloon angioplasty, reducing the portosystemic gradient from 15 to 10 mmHg, and embolization of a gastric varix. A large-volume paracentesis removed 5 liters of fluid, with no signs of infection. He received one unit of packed red blood cells, and his hemoglobin stabilized. Chest pain was attributed to esophagitis and a hiatal hernia, with no cardiac cause. Hyponatremia remained stable on fluid restriction. He improved clinically, was discharged home on pantoprazole twice daily and sucralfate, with follow-up planned with hepatology and palliative care.
